subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
vignette: A 34-year-old woman with polycythemia vera presents with 2 weeks of progressive abdominal distention and right upper quadrant pain. Examination shows marked hepatomegaly, ascites, and dilated abdominal wall veins; there is no jugular venous distention. Liver imaging reveals a mottled nutmeg appearance and thrombosis of the hepatic veins.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's liver findings?

options.text: Thrombosis of the portal vein proximal to the liver
Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow with centrilobular congestion and necrosis
Fibrous bands and regenerative nodules from chronic alcohol use
Diffuse infiltration of the liver by metastatic carcinoma
Elevated right atrial pressure from right-sided heart failure

explanation_correct: Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow tract obstruction (eg, thrombosis or compression) producing centrilobular congestion and necrosis and thus congestive liver disease with hepatomegaly, ascites, varices, abdominal pain, and liver failure. Hypercoagulable states such as polycythemia vera are classic associations. Absence of jugular venous distention helps distinguish it from cardiac causes of congestive hepatopathy. The mottled nutmeg appearance reflects the underlying congestion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Portal vein thrombosis occurs proximal to the liver, is usually asymptomatic, and does not produce centrilobular congestion or a nutmeg liver.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alcoholic cirrhosis produces regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands, not acute hepatic venous outflow obstruction with hepatic vein thrombosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metastases are the most common malignant liver tumors overall but are usually multiple deposits and do not cause hepatic vein thrombosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Right-sided heart failure can cause congestive hepatopathy but would be expected to produce jugular venous distention, which is absent here.

educationalObjective: Budd-Chiari is hepatic venous outflow obstruction causing centrilobular congestion, hepatomegaly, ascites, and no jugular venous distention, associated with hypercoagulable states.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
vignette: A 28-year-old woman develops tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and mild jaundice 6 weeks after delivery. Doppler ultrasound shows absent flow in the hepatic veins with a patent inferior vena cava and normal right ventricular function. Her neck veins are flat.
question: Which of the following best accounts for the absence of jugular venous distention in this patient?

options.text: Ascites lowers intra-abdominal pressure and enhances venous return
Portal hypertension shunts blood away from the systemic circulation
The obstruction lies in the hepatic venous outflow tract, so right atrial pressure remains normal
Reduced hepatic synthetic function masks the signs of venous congestion
Postpartum hypercoagulability prevents pressure transmission to the inferior vena cava

explanation_correct: In Budd-Chiari syndrome the obstruction is within the hepatic venous outflow tract (thrombosis or compression), downstream from the liver but proximal to right atrial filling, so hepatic venous pressure rises while right atrial pressure and jugular venous distention do not. The postpartum state is a classic hypercoagulable association. Centrilobular congestion and necrosis produce hepatomegaly, ascites, varices, abdominal pain, and liver failure. A nutmeg liver may be seen.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ascites does not lower intra-abdominal pressure; it is a consequence of increased hepatic sinusoidal pressure.
explanation_incorrect.B: Portal hypertension promotes collateral vessel and varix formation but does not decompress the right atrium or explain flat neck veins.
explanation_incorrect.D: Impaired synthesis lowers albumin and promotes edema and ascites, but it is not why jugular venous distention is absent in outflow obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypercoagulability promotes venous thrombosis; it does not mechanically block transmission of pressure to the inferior vena cava.

educationalObjective: Distinguish Budd-Chiari from cardiac congestive hepatopathy by the level of obstruction and the absence of jugular venous distention.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
vignette: A 56-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis undergoes routine CT imaging that shows a thrombus in the portal vein proximal to the liver. He reports mild intermittent abdominal pain and low-grade fever but has no new hepatomegaly.
question: Which of the following is most characteristic of this condition?

options.text: It invariably produces massive hepatomegaly and a nutmeg liver
It most often presents with sudden painless jaundice and acholic stools
It is usually severely symptomatic with right upper quadrant pain in most patients
It is usually asymptomatic but may cause portal hypertension, abdominal pain, and fever
It typically results from hepatic vein thrombosis due to polycythemia vera

explanation_correct: Portal vein thrombosis is thrombosis in the portal vein proximal to the liver. It is usually asymptomatic in the majority of patients, but it is associated with portal hypertension, abdominal pain, and fever. Etiologies include cirrhosis, malignancy, pancreatitis, and sepsis. If the thrombus extends to the superior mesenteric vein, it may lead to bowel ischemia. Unlike Budd-Chiari, hepatomegaly is absent unless preexisting liver disease is present.

explanation_incorrect.A: Nutmeg liver and prominent hepatomegaly are features of Budd-Chiari (hepatic venous outflow obstruction), not portal vein thrombosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Painless jaundice with pale stools suggests biliary obstruction or cholestasis, such as choledocholithiasis or pancreatic cancer, rather than portal vein thrombosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Most patients with portal vein thrombosis are asymptomatic; severe right upper quadrant pain is not the typical presentation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hepatic vein thrombosis with polycythemia vera is Budd-Chiari syndrome, which involves a different vascular bed.

educationalObjective: Portal vein thrombosis is often asymptomatic, linked to cirrhosis/malignancy/pancreatitis/sepsis, and may extend to the superior mesenteric vein causing bowel ischemia.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis and a large volume of ascites presents with 1 day of fever, chills, and diffuse abdominal pain. Paracentesis yields cloudy fluid with an absolute neutrophil count of 390 cells/mm3 and no surgical cause is found.
question: Which of the following organisms is most likely to be isolated from this patient's ascitic fluid?

options.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae as the sole common cause
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Candida albicans
Hepatitis B virus
Escherichia coli or Klebsiella species

explanation_correct: This patient has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, a common and potentially fatal bacterial infection in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. It is commonly caused by gram-negative organisms such as E coli and Klebsiella; gram-positive Streptococcus is a less common cause. Diagnosis is by paracentesis with ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3. Empiric first-line therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin.

explanation_incorrect.A: Streptococcus is a less common cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; gram-negative enteric organisms predominate.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tuberculous peritonitis produces a chronic lymphocytic rather than neutrophilic ascitic fluid and is not the typical acute spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Candida is not a common cause of community-acquired spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hepatitis B virus is a cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, not bacterial peritonitis.

educationalObjective: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic ascites is usually caused by gram-negative enteric organisms (E coli, Klebsiella) with ascitic ANC above 250 cells/mm3.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
vignette: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with new confusion and low-grade fever. Ascitic fluid analysis shows an absolute neutrophil count of 460 cells/mm3. No other infectious source is identified.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Ceftriaxone
Oral metronidazole alone
Intravenous acyclovir
Topical clotrimazole
Oral lactulose

explanation_correct: Empiric first-line treatment of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, which covers the common gram-negative enteric organisms. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is often asymptomatic but can cause fevers, chills, abdominal pain, ileus, or worsening encephalopathy. Diagnosis requires paracentesis with an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3. It is a common and potentially fatal infection in cirrhosis with ascites.

explanation_incorrect.B: Metronidazole alone does not adequately cover the gram-negative enteric organisms that commonly cause spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acyclovir is an antiviral agent for herpesviruses and has no role in treating bacterial peritonitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Clotrimazole is a topical antifungal and would not treat a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lactulose is used for hepatic encephalopathy by increasing NH4+ trapping, not as antimicrobial therapy for peritonitis.

educationalObjective: A third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) is first-line empiric therapy for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
